title: Characterization of Hydroxyls in Surface Oxide of Superconducting Tantalum and Their Mitigation in Quantum Circuits
authors: Ekta Bhatia, Nicholas Pieniazek, Aleksandra Biedron, Sandra Schujman, Hunter Frost, Zhihao Xiao, Jakub Nalaskowski, Kevin Musick, Thomas Murray, Satyavolu Papa Rao
abstract: Recently, tantalum (Ta) has gained attention in superconducting quantum circuits due to the longer coherence times achieved when replacing niobium (Nb) in capacitor pads. Previous literature shows that surface oxides that form upon ambient exposure on superconducting metals such as Ta, Al, and Nb host two-level system (TLS) defects, which are a leading source of microwave loss and decoherence. While the surface oxides of Nb and Al have been extensively studied, Ta oxides remain less well understood. Using secondary ion mass spectrometry of alpha-Ta films deposited at 300 mm wafer scale, we show for the first time that hydroxyls accumulate in the Ta suboxide region above the underlying Ta. Angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows that the surface region is dominated by Ta2O5, with sub-stoichiometric TaOx present in between the Ta2O5 and underlying Ta. The thickness of the tantalum oxide is confirmed by transmission electron microscopy. We demonstrate that [OH] incorporation can be suppressed by replacing the native oxide with an oxide formed during chemical mechanical planarization of alpha-Ta films. Our findings support the hypothesis that TLS defects are non-uniform within the oxide thickness and suggest hydroxyls as a probable molecular origin of these loss channels. Furthermore, we show the feasibility of plasma nitridization as a method to decrease hydroxyl loading on alpha-Ta surfaces. The modulation of hydroxyl content through surface engineering of alpha-Ta can enable the fabrication of more robust, high-coherence superconducting quantum circuits by addressing a potential TLS source.
summary: This experimental study characterizes the formation of hydroxyl defects within the surface oxides of superconducting Tantalum. Using SIMS and ARXPS, the authors prove that these hydroxyl groups are major contributors to decoherence sources in quantum circuits. They demonstrate that modifying the oxide layer via CMP or plasma nitridization can effectively suppress this defect concentration.
main_problem: Surface oxides on superconducting Tantalum (Ta) host Two-Level System (TLS) defects, which are a primary source of microwave loss and decoherence in quantum circuits.
main_result: The accumulation of hydroxyls ([OH]) in the suboxide region is confirmed, and surface engineering techniques like Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) or plasma nitridization can suppress this hydroxyl loading to improve coherence.
method: The study employs advanced characterization techniques including Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS), Angle-resolved X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (ARXPS), and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM).
model_or_system: The physical system is superconducting Tantalum ($\alpha$-Ta) films coated with native or engineered surface oxides ($	ext{Ta}_2	ext{O}_5$, $	ext{TaO}_x$). The focus is on the molecular defects, specifically hydroxyls, within this oxide layer.
key_observables: Depth profiles of oxide species ($	ext{Ta}_2	ext{O}_5$, $	ext{TaOH}$), total maximum $	ext{TaOH}^-/	ext{Total}$ signal intensity across different treatments.
important_parameters: Superconducting temperature regime, surface treatment type (native vs. CMP vs. nitridized), and oxide thickness.
main_assumptions: The TLS defects are molecularly linked to the presence of hydroxyl groups within the non-uniform oxide structure; mitigation via surface chemistry is feasible.
figures_summary: Figures show ARXPS analysis confirming stratified oxidation states, SIMS depth profiles quantifying $	ext{TaOH}$ accumulation in suboxides, and comparative plots demonstrating that CMP or nitridization reduces the maximum hydroxyl signal intensity.
paper_structure: The paper systematically characterizes the oxide structure using ARXPS/TEM, then uses SIMS to map out the chemical species ($	ext{Ta}_2	ext{O}_5$, $	ext{TaOH}$) across depth. It culminates by comparing native vs. engineered oxides (CMP, nitridization) to quantify hydroxyl suppression.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical material science bottleneck for superconducting qubits and quantum devices by identifying a specific molecular defect source (hydroxyls) and providing actionable surface engineering solutions.
